lead: This entry covers two separate practices that looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities group together: prolonged food fasting (going beyond 24 hours without eating, often 5 to 20 days) and 'dopamine fasting', in which a person abstains from stimulating behaviours such as phone use, gaming or pornography.[1][2] People use extended fasts to lose body fat quickly, since lower body fat is widely said to reveal jawline, cheekbones and neck definition. People use dopamine fasting to build self-control and free up time and focus for gym, sleep and skincare habits.[2]

Dopamine fasting was developed as a cognitive behavioural approach by California psychologist Cameron Sepah and attracted media coverage from late 2019.[2] Sepah says the aim is to reduce impulsive behaviours rather than literally lower dopamine, and that the name is misleading; some neuroscientists have criticised the idea that the brain can be 'reset' this way.[2]

Fasting research focuses on metabolic effects such as ketosis and weight loss, and clinicians document risks of prolonged fasts, including refeeding syndrome.[1] Neither practice has been studied for facial appearance.

chain: Extended fast creates a large calorie deficit
Sharper jaw, cheeks and neck; separately, less impulsive screen use leaves time for appearance habits
angle.text: Extended fasting is used for rapid fat loss, which people say sharpens facial definition. Dopamine fasting is used to cut time-consuming impulsive habits, in the hope of more consistent training, sleep and skincare.

infobox: More than 24 hours, often 5 to 20 days[1]
Smartphones, social media, gaming, gambling, shopping, emotional eating, pornography[2]

paras: The practice was first developed by Cameron Sepah as a form of cognitive behavioural therapy and is associated with Silicon Valley.[2] Targets named in coverage include smartphones, social media, gaming, gambling, shopping, emotional eating and pornography, and versions vary in strictness.[2] Proponents describe gains in self-control and encourage lower-stimulation activities such as reading or outdoor sports.[2]

Harvard psychiatrist Peter Grinspoon called Sepah's approach sensible but not new, and criticised ever more extreme versions (Harvard Health Blog, February 2020).[2] University of Reading neuroscientist Ciara McCabe disputed the idea that avoiding a stimulus resets the brain, and UConn's John Salamone described the practice as nebulously defined.[2]
A 2022 paper in Lifestyle Medicine examined it as a possible intervention for behavioural addiction, and a 2024 study found higher screen time associated with higher impulsivity.[2]

In prolonged fasting the body shifts from glucose production to ketosis, and electrolytes such as sodium, potassium and magnesium fall. Reported weight loss is rapid, with roughly two-thirds of early loss being lean tissue. The article reports no sound clinical evidence that fasting extends human lifespan.[1]

Documented risks include refeeding syndrome, which can occur after about 4 to 5 days without food and can be fatal, and gallstones. Prolonged fasts have been done under medical supervision, for example a 382-day case in 1965 to 1966.[1] Fasting for fat loss is also discussed in online communities, for example a Hacker News thread in which a user describes fat loss experiments combining water fasting with ChatGPT.[3]
Dopamine fasting was covered by Vice (October 2019) and the New York Times (November 2019), and later by Marie Claire, Harvard Health and others.[2]
No studies found testing either practice for facial appearance. General research is limited to broader fasting and behavioural-addiction literature summarised above.[1][2]

name: Extended fasting / dopamine fasts

card.summary: Abstaining from food or stimulation to 'reset'; the behavioural version is loosely defined and extended fasting carries real medical risks.
card.note: Refeeding syndrome after prolonged fasting can be fatal.

quick.overview:
Two practices share this entry: multi-day food fasting, and dopamine fasting, where people avoid stimulating habits such as phones or gaming.

No studies were found on appearance outcomes, and experts quoted in coverage dispute the 'reset' framing of dopamine fasting.
quick.mechanism: Extended fasting shifts the body into ketosis. Dopamine fasting is described by its originator as reducing impulsive behaviour, not lowering dopamine itself.
quick.risks: Prolonged fasting can cause electrolyte loss, gallstones, lean-mass loss and refeeding syndrome, which can be fatal. Dopamine fasting has no specific physical harms reported, though critics call its premise unscientific.
